title: Mini Nuclear Is a Promise. Your Roof Is a Power Plant.
subtitle: Solar Is the Smarter Bet — the Prosper point of view
format: Prosper News editorial commentary / earnest video essay

hooks.text: Mini nuclear is a promise. Your roof can be a power plant. Our position at Prosper is simple: put working solar and thoughtfully designed storage ahead of waiting on a reactor announcement. I'm Hannah, Prosper's AI presenter. A confident face on a screen isn't evidence, so let's put the evidence on the screen.

This is the line at the top of our Prosper News article: Solar is the smarter bet. We mean it. Nuclear developers can make their pitch. But families deserve more than a future completion date. They deserve a practical look at what their roof produces, what their utility charges, and what storage could change.

If your solar stopped producing tomorrow, would you know? That's a more useful question for your household than whether a proposed reactor might become affordable years from now. At Prosper, we want solar that works, storage with a clear job, and numbers you can inspect. Let's explain why that's our bet.

scenes.title: The opening: make the position unmistakable
scenes.performance: Direct eye contact. Calm conviction. Pause after the first two sentences; no excited sales pitch.
scenes.visual: Open on the existing Prosper News / Now Live card for two seconds. Cut to the approved Hannah avatar, waist-up, in a cream-and-Prosper-blue editorial set. Keep the real Prosper logo visible.
scenes.narration:
Mini nuclear is a promise. Your roof can be a power plant.

Our position at Prosper is simple: put working solar and thoughtfully designed storage ahead of waiting on a reactor announcement.

I'm Hannah, Prosper's AI presenter. A confident face on a screen isn't evidence, so let's put the evidence on the screen.

We want to know what a technology delivers, what it costs, and when it starts helping the people paying the bills.

That standard applies to a nuclear developer. It applies to a solar company. And it absolutely applies to Prosper.

Because the interesting question isn't who has the most impressive promise. It's what can make your home work better.
scenes.retention: Cold verdict, presenter disclosure, and a common accountability standard. Plant the promise-versus-performance contrast.

scenes.title: What we mean by mini nuclear
scenes.performance: Fair description of the pitch, followed by firm scrutiny. Critique the proposal, not engineers or people who support nuclear.
scenes.visual: Original, plainly labeled proposal graphic: design → financing → licensing → construction → operating electricity. Reveal one stage at a time. No invented developer logo or fabricated project footage.
screen: A PROPOSAL HAS TO BECOME A POWER PLANT.
scenes.narration:
Mini nuclear usually means small modular reactors: designs intended to deliver nuclear power in smaller units, with more factory-built components.

The pitch is that smaller, repeatable designs could improve delivery. That's a proposition worth examining. It isn't a result we should assume.

A proposed reactor still needs a credible route through financing, licensing, construction, and operation. The schedule matters. The final bill matters. Who carries the risk matters.

We're not saying nuclear physics is imaginary. We're saying an announcement and a dependable energy solution for your household are very different things.

And we're not comfortable telling a family to put practical improvements on hold while someone else's project works through that list.

Show the delivery. Then make the argument.
scenes.retention: Define the target precisely: the promised delivery case, not whether nuclear energy exists.

scenes.title: The receipts: Vogtle
scenes.performance: Slow down for dates and dollar amounts. Allow reading time. Focus criticism on delivery and accountability.
scenes.visual: Hannah in picture-in-picture beside a reconstruction of the article's Vogtle table. Reveal original estimates first, then operating dates and reported cost. Label the comparison historical.
scenes.narration:
Let's start with a real project: the two-reactor expansion at Plant Vogtle in Georgia.

And before we point at someone else's sales pitch, remember: Prosper's proposals should be held to their numbers, too.

According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, Vogtle's expansion was originally expected to cost fourteen billion dollars. Unit Three was expected to begin operating in twenty sixteen, and Unit Four in twenty seventeen.

Unit Three began commercial operation in July twenty twenty-three. Unit Four followed in April twenty twenty-four. The cost reported by the agency was more than thirty billion dollars.

Vogtle is a large-reactor project, not an example of an operating small modular reactor. It doesn't tell us what every future design will cost.

It does show why we ask hard questions when a new nuclear project is presented as an affordability solution.

Optimism is not a cost-control system.
scenes.retention: First concrete evidence payoff. Separate the historical large-reactor example from SMR forecasts.

scenes.title: The test every promise should pass
scenes.performance: Conversational and probing, like walking a homeowner through a proposal.
scenes.visual: Four questions appear beside Hannah. Keep each readable for at least four seconds. End on the electricity-delivery question.
screen: WHAT CAN WE BUILD IN THE MEANTIME?
scenes.narration:
So here's the test we'd put in front of any new reactor proposal.

What is the full cost, including financing? What's the credible operating date? Who absorbs the overrun? And what could a realistic combination of solar, storage, efficiency, and grid improvements deliver during the same period?

That last question is important. A project can have good lifetime emissions and still arrive too late to be the strongest response to today's problem.

Solar projects can face delays, too. Nobody gets to compare a perfect solar schedule with a troubled nuclear schedule and call that fair.

Compare real alternatives, with real constraints.

Our opinion is that solar and storage have earned priority through the progress they've already delivered. A future reactor should have to earn its place through the same kind of evidence.
scenes.retention: Turn criticism into a reusable decision framework.

scenes.title: Why solar and storage earned our confidence
scenes.performance: Confident, with a clear pause before the household-price distinction. The chart is evidence, not a retail discount.
scenes.visual: Two-panel graphic using cited article figures. Solar and batteries stay in separate panels with different units and prominent utility-scale labels.
screen: Around 95% lower installed four-hour utility-battery cost since 2010
Source: IRENA · Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2025
scenes.narration:
Look at the cost history.

The International Renewable Energy Agency reports a global average of forty-four dollars per megawatt-hour for new utility-scale solar commissioned in twenty twenty-five. That's eighty-nine percent below twenty ten.

Its estimate for installed four-hour utility-scale batteries is around ninety-five percent below twenty ten.

Those are different measures, and neither is a price quote for your house. They tell us something about the record of the technologies.

Solar modules, batteries, installation methods, and controls can improve through repeated manufacturing and engineering. That progress has already happened at substantial scale.

Prices don't fall every quarter. In fact, that solar-generation average was flat against the previous year. Financing and local installation costs still matter.

Our confidence doesn't depend on a fantasy of endless price drops. It comes from a history of equipment getting more capable and more affordable.
scenes.retention: A positive case with bounded, labeled figures; avoid implying retail savings.

scenes.title: Storage is already operating
scenes.performance: Emphasize 'operating.' Make the power-versus-stored-energy distinction clear.
scenes.visual: Count-up stops at Nearly 52 GW. Below it: U.S. utility-scale battery power capacity · June 2026. Observation date stays visible throughout.
screen: U.S. utility-scale battery power capacity · June 2026
8.3 GW added in the first half of 2026
Power capacity ≠ stored energy or backup duration
scenes.narration:
Storage also has an operating record you can count.

In its August twenty twenty-six update, the Energy Information Administration reported nearly fifty-two gigawatts of operating utility-scale battery power capacity in the United States by June.

Operators had added eight-point-three gigawatts in the first half of the year.

That number describes power capacity. It doesn't tell you how many hours the fleet could support a particular load, and it isn't a count of home batteries.

But it matters to this debate because we're talking about equipment reported as operating, not only projects announced for the future.

A plan is useful. A completed installation is stronger evidence.

That's the distinction we want homeowners to keep making, whether they're hearing about a reactor, a solar project, or a battery on their own wall.
scenes.retention: Replay promise versus performance with completed storage additions.

scenes.title: The credibility check: nuclear is low-carbon, too
scenes.performance: Level and unhurried. An honest qualification that strengthens the argument.
scenes.visual: Use the article's life-cycle emissions chart. Keep NREL 2021 attribution and literature-median caveat visible. Do not crop out nuclear's lower median.
scenes.narration:
Here's something a serious pro-solar argument should say out loud: nuclear is also a low-carbon source of electricity.

In the life-cycle research compilation shown in our article, nuclear's median emissions are lower than solar's. We show that chart because facts don't become inconvenient just because they complicate a headline.

Solar manufacturing has a footprint. Glass, metals, silicon, transport, and eventual recycling all belong in the accounting.

Existing nuclear plants can provide valuable clean electricity. Closing one and replacing its output with fossil generation can work against the goal.

Our criticism is aimed at treating new nuclear promises as the default answer to affordability and near-term household needs.

We favor solar and storage because of their delivery record and the control they can put closer to the customer. We don't need to pretend another technology has no value to make that case.
scenes.retention: Midpoint credibility pivot: acknowledge the counterpoint and sharpen the real thesis.

scenes.title: Yes, the sun goes down. Design for it.
scenes.performance: Matter-of-fact. Explain the distinction without sounding defensive or technical for its own sake.
scenes.visual: Simple original diagram: sunlight → solar → home; excess generation → battery; battery → selected home loads later. Add kW and kWh labels separately. Show a proper backup configuration as a separate requirement, not an automatic feature.
screen: kW = power available at one time
Outage backup requires the right system design
scenes.narration:
Yes, the sun goes down. That's a design requirement, not a revelation.

A battery can store energy for later. Whether that helps with evening use, a particular rate schedule, or an outage depends on the system and the job you give it.

Two measurements matter. Kilowatts describe power: how much equipment the system can supply at once. Kilowatt-hours describe energy: how much it stores.

Think of flow and tank size. A large tank doesn't guarantee enough flow to start every appliance. A strong flow doesn't tell you how long the tank will last.

And ordinary grid-connected solar generally shuts down during an outage. Keeping selected loads running requires a compatible backup design and the right equipment.

The question isn't simply, do you have a battery?

It's, what was your system designed to do?
scenes.retention: Answer the obvious objection and give the viewer a useful two-unit distinction.

scenes.title: Before you add storage, check the solar.
scenes.performance: Practical and helpful. Let the battery-does-not-fix-solar line land without talking over it.
scenes.visual: Illustrative monitoring dashboard clearly labeled Example, not customer data. Show production history, an alert, twelve months of bills, then a qualified technician. Optional very short Baby Mr. Electric reaction cutaway; return immediately to Hannah.
screen: IS YOUR SOLAR DOING ITS JOB?
Production history · Alerts · Bills · Service support
A BATTERY DOESN'T FIX A SOLAR-PRODUCTION FAULT.
scenes.narration:
If you already have solar, start with the system you own.

Can you see its production history? Are alerts being answered? Does its output make sense for the season and the system's design?

Bring together the monitoring record, your original system information, and twelve months of electricity bills.

A bigger bill alone doesn't prove the panels failed. Your usage or rates may have changed. A blank monitoring screen can be a communications problem rather than a generation problem.

But guessing isn't a service plan.

Have a qualified professional investigate the issue and explain the findings. Ask who handles the repair, whether a warranty applies, and what happens next. Don't climb onto the roof or open electrical equipment to investigate it yourself.

A battery doesn't fix a solar-production fault.

Make the solar work. Then decide what storage should add.
scenes.retention: Shift from industry debate to an immediate homeowner action; memorable warning.

scenes.title: Give the battery a job—and make the numbers answer.
scenes.performance: Sharp on bad projections, constructive on the homeowner's choices. Avoid a universal savings promise.
scenes.visual: Three job cards: evening energy, rate management, selected-load backup. An illustrative proposal checklist shows actual tariff, export rules, compatibility, capacity, output, installed cost, financing, and remaining utility charges. Optional muted fox cutaway symbolizes a rate problem only.
screen: Evening energy · Rate management · Selected-load backup
Rates, export rules, eligibility and results vary.
scenes.narration:
Now give the battery a job.

Do you want to use more of your solar after sunset? Manage an expensive time-of-use period? Keep selected essentials running during an outage?

Those goals can overlap, but they don't always call for the same settings or system size.

Start with your actual utility tariff and export rules. Check compatibility with your existing equipment. Compare usable energy, power output, installed cost, financing, and the utility charges that would remain.

Prosper's storage page is a place to start that conversation. A product logo isn't a finished design, and a big number on a brochure isn't a household savings calculation.

Ask for the assumptions in writing.

If the math doesn't fit your house, the responsible answer is to change the plan, not decorate the projection.

That's the standard we want you to bring to us.
scenes.retention: Replace vague battery enthusiasm with a specific decision and demand for transparent assumptions.

scenes.title: The grid still matters.
scenes.performance: Clear-eyed. Do not imply rooftop solar avoids all approvals or that utility-scale queue figures apply to household installations.
scenes.visual: Grid connection diagram with transmission-scale project queue and household interconnection shown as distinct categories. Keep study scope visible next to the queue statistic.
screen: BUILDING EQUIPMENT ISN'T THE WHOLE JOB.
Transmission-project study: median over five years
Projects completed in 2025 · Regions with available data
scenes.narration:
There's another part of delivery that gets lost in energy arguments: connecting the equipment.

Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's twenty twenty-six queue report found a median wait of more than five years for transmission-connected projects completed in twenty twenty-five, in the regions with available data.

That's a transmission-project finding. It is not a prediction that your rooftop installation will take five years.

But it explains why buying hardware isn't the same thing as delivering a working energy system.

Household projects can also need utility review, permits, and inspections. The requirements depend on the location and design.

We want better connections, practical controls, and more effective permitting alongside solar and storage.

Local energy can put useful equipment closer to the load. It doesn't make every grid constraint or approval disappear.
scenes.retention: Broaden the practical delivery test and inoculate against an overclaim about rooftop timelines.

scenes.title: Count the whole lifecycle.
scenes.performance: Serious, not ominous. No disaster music or imagery that implies unsupported health claims.
scenes.visual: Two balanced lifecycle strips. Solar: manufacturing → operation → reuse/recycling. Nuclear: fuel → operation → spent-fuel management. Use neutral symbols; no mushroom clouds, glowing waste, or fake measurements.
scenes.narration:
We also care about what a technology requires over its full life.

Photovoltaic solar doesn't need the thermal cooling process used by many large power plants. That gives it an operational water advantage in many comparisons, though manufacturing and site maintenance still have impacts.

Nuclear creates spent fuel that requires carefully managed handling and storage, with long-term disposal responsibilities. Properly managed storage is a regulated protection system, not evidence that everyone nearby is in danger.

And solar doesn't get a free pass at the end of its life. Panels, batteries, and other equipment need responsible handling, reuse where appropriate, and recycling pathways.

The useful argument is about the actual requirements and who is accountable for them.

We prefer solutions that can be delivered, maintained, and responsibly managed—not a marketing story that stops when the installation photo is taken.
scenes.retention: Address long-term objections without fearmongering, and connect responsibility back to aftercare.

scenes.title: What a good Prosper plan should contain.
scenes.performance: Warm, specific, accountable. These are standards to request, not claims that every service is already included.
scenes.visual: Three-step plan with legible deliverables: 1. Check performance. 2. Define storage. 3. Name the support owner. Show the live article's system-check section and service links, not a fabricated customer proposal.
screen: Request scope, costs, assumptions and support terms in writing.
scenes.narration:
Here's what we'd like a good conversation with Prosper to produce.

First, a clear picture of what your solar is doing today. Not just how many panels are on the roof, but what they produce and what your bills show.

Second, a storage plan with a defined purpose: the loads you care about, the energy and power required, the backup configuration if you want it, and the complete cost.

Third, a clear answer about support. Who monitors the system, if monitoring is included? Who responds to a problem? What do the warranties cover? Can you access your records and see what's happening?

Availability, incentives, approvals, and timing depend on the project. Have those details confirmed for your home.

The promise isn't that every house gets the same answer.

It's the standard we should all insist on: the system has to keep earning its place on your home.
scenes.retention: Deliver the homeowner checklist promised by the talk; turn the opinion into an accountable service standard.

scenes.title: Powering more than your home.
scenes.performance: Slow slightly. Sincere, community-minded, not a swelling corporate speech. Pause between the two lines from the supplied graphic.
scenes.visual: Bring in Craig's supplied community graphic, uncropped and readable, on a black background. Preserve its white-and-teal wording as supplied. Optional very brief Prosper Shield versus Sly Fox character beat as a brand metaphor only; no legacy end card.
scenes.narration:
Powering more than your home. Powering our community.

That's the direction we want Prosper to stand for.

It starts with a family understanding its energy system, knowing where to get help, and being able to question a proposal without feeling lost.

Then those questions travel. A neighbor learns to check production. A friend asks what a battery will actually run. Another family learns that a warranty and a working service relationship aren't the same thing.

That's a community benefit we can help build: better information, clearer expectations, and people looking out for one another.

The slogan doesn't mean every home battery can power the neighborhood. It means the responsibility should extend beyond making a sale.

Equipment matters. So does who stands behind it.
scenes.retention: Human-stakes payoff tied directly to the user's community artwork without implying a neighborhood microgrid.

scenes.title: The close: evidence, then action.
scenes.performance: Return to the directness of the opening. Warm invitation, not urgency. Leave the final card up long enough to read.
scenes.visual: Hannah full frame, then the Prosper News card with the live article URL and Read the research / Check your solar / Explore storage. End with the community graphic or Prosper logo. Hold the final card six seconds.
screen: Read the research · Check your solar · Explore storage
scenes.narration:
So here's our position.

Prioritize working solar. Add storage where it does a useful job. Improve efficiency and connections. Make every competing proposal prove its cost, timing, and value.

If a future reactor earns its case with evidence, examine the evidence. Until then, homeowners shouldn't have to confuse somebody else's promise with a plan for their own roof.

You don't have to take my digital word for it. Read the sources. Bring your numbers. Ask the questions.

You'll find the full article, research links, and ways to discuss solar performance and storage at news dot Prosper Shield dot I O.

Mini nuclear is a promise. Your roof can be a power plant.

Solar and storage first. Keep them working. Take your power back.

Powering more than your home. Powering our community.
scenes.retention: Replay the opening contrast, resolve the practical question, and give one spoken destination.

sources.title: U.S. NRC — High-Level Waste
sources.supports: Spent nuclear fuel and high-level waste require regulated handling and storage and long-term disposal management. Not evidence of an unqualified danger to nearby residents.

production.status: Script and production plan only. No avatar, voice, video render, upload or publication performed.
production.editorial: Prosper commercial editorial commentary: explicitly pro-solar and pro-storage, skeptical of new mini-nuclear delivery and affordability promises. Not a claim that nuclear physics is imaginary, that no SMRs operate anywhere, or that solar plus a home battery replaces all firm grid generation.
production.host: Use Hannah as requested. Label the host Hannah · AI presenter. Use only an approved likeness and voice; this script does not authorize cloning a person's identity. No invented personal experience, credentials or customer testimonials.
production.delivery: Target 145 spoken words per minute, calm conviction, short pauses for figures. Timings are estimates, not rendered measurements. The scene transition allowance is 3 seconds each, with an additional 3 seconds for the final card. Short optional cutaways play under the narration, not as added runtime.
production.format: 16:9 master, preferably 1920×1080. The supplied clips are 1280×720; avoid implying they are native 1080p/4K. Keep important text and faces within safe margins for later social crops. Export shorter versions only after the full argument remains accurate.
production.brand: Match the live news site: cream #f9f4ed, Prosper blue #0b5cff, acid yellow #f4ff00, ink #141414; existing Prosper logo; Fander display / Geist body where available. Preserve the supplied black/white/teal community graphic as provided. Keep evidence pages clean and legible.
production.cadence: Start with the argument immediately. Change visual emphasis every 10–20 seconds as useful, not on a rigid timer. Give statistics reading time. No dramatic nuclear-disaster footage or fake before-and-after bills. Character humor is optional and brief.
production.audio: Use the approved Hannah voice. Narration stays dominant over restrained music. Do not use unreviewed audio from the attached MOVs. Spell out numbers in the spoken script; show conventional numeric units on screen.
pronunciation: IRENA: eye-REE-nah; the script uses the agency's full name.
Kilowatt-hours and kilowatts are intentionally different.
Spoken URL: news dot Prosper Shield dot I O.
production.rights: Keep source attributions with charts and figures. Prefer original reconstructions from cited data over reusing third-party footage. Verify any third-party visual and music permissions before rendering. User-provided originals remain untouched.
factualBoundaries: Vogtle is historical large-reactor evidence, not an SMR project or a prediction for every future reactor.
Utility-scale global cost figures are not residential installed prices or savings estimates.
GW measures battery power, not energy capacity, discharge hours, or number of homes backed up.
Nuclear is also low-carbon; preserve the nuclear comparison in the cited lifecycle chart.
Queue duration is from transmission-connected projects, not a quoted wait for rooftop customers.
Backup requires the proper design. Never promise whole-home or multi-day backup without a project-specific load/energy analysis.
No fixed savings, rebates, credits, eligibility, installation date, service coverage or financing terms are promised.
Community wording does not claim automatic neighborhood backup, energy sharing, grid-service enrollment or payment.
Service questions are standards to ask Prosper to document, not representations that every service is already included.
production.clipReview: Video metadata and five frames per clip were inspected. Full clip audio was not reviewed or transcribed. Cutaway suggestions are editorial candidates only; no precise edit points or final video approval are claimed.
